clad.e: From Middle English clad, cladde, cled(e), cledde, past tense and past participle forms of clethen (“(also figurative) to put clothing on, clothe, dress; to provide clothing to; to arm, equip; to cover, envelop; to conceal; to adorn”), from Old English clǣþan (past tense clǣþde, *clædde).

claim.e: From Middle English claimen, borrowed from Old French clamer (“to call, name, send for”), from Latin clāmō, clāmāre (“to call, cry out”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to shout”), which is imitative.
claim.g: A demand of ownership made for something.

clamor.e: Recorded in English since c. 1385, as Middle English clamour, from Old French clamor (modern clameur), from Latin clāmor (“a shout, cry”), from clāmō (“cry out, complain”). The verb sense "to silence" may have a distinct (unknown) etymology.
clamor.g: A great outcry or vociferation; loud and continued shouting or exclamation.

clamorous.e: From clamor + -ous; compare Latin clāmōrōsus and French clamoreux (obsolete), from Latin clāmōrem.

clamour.e: From Latin clāmor (“a shout, cry”), from clāmō (“cry out, complain”).
clamour.g: UK and Canada standard spelling of clamor.

clan.e: Borrowed from Irish clann (“offspring, children of the family”) and Scottish Gaelic clann, both from Old Irish cland, borrowed from Old Welsh plant, itself borrowed from Latin planta (“shoot, offspring”).
clan.g: A group of people all descended from a common ancestor, in fact or belief, especially when the exact genealogies are not known.

clang.g: A loud, ringing sound, like that made by free-hanging metal objects striking each other; usually, one considered more jarring than melodious

clap.e: From Middle English clappen, from Old English clæppan, *clappian, from Proto-West Germanic *klappijan, *klappōn, from Proto-Germanic *klappōną (“to clap”).
clap.g: The act of striking the palms of the hands, or any two surfaces, together.

clap.e: Uncertain. Probably from Old French clapoir (“bubo, inflammation from infection”), from clapier (“brothel”). May also be from old, unsafe treatments for gonorrhea, such as clapping the penis between a book and a hard surface to break up obstructions in the urethra and permit urination.

clash.g: A loud sound, like the crashing together of metal objects; a crash.

clasp.e: Noun dated ca. 1300 and verb dated ca. 1400; from Middle English claspe (“metal catch or hook used to hold things together”), possible metathesis of clapse, which comes from or related to Old English clyppan (“clasp”) (also see clip (verb)).
clasp.g: A device with interlocking parts used for fastening things together, such as a fastener or a holder.

class.e: From Middle French classe, from Latin classis (“a class or division of the people, assembly of people, the whole body of citizens called to arms, the army, the fleet, later a class or division in general”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”).
class.g: A group, collection, category or set sharing characteristics or attributes.

classify.e: From French classifier. By surface analysis, class + -ify.
classify.g: to identify by or divide into classes; to categorize

clatter.e: From Middle English clatren (“to make a rattling sound”), from Old English *clatrian (attested as the Late Old English gerund clatrung), of onomatopoeic origin. The noun, derived from the verb, is first attested in the 14ᵗʰ century.

clave.e: From Spanish clave, from Latin clāvis (“key”).
clave.g: A characteristic pattern of beats, especially the 3-2 son clave.

claw.e: From Middle English clawe, from Old English clawu, from Proto-Germanic *klawō.
claw.g: A curved, pointed, horny projection on each digit of the foot of a mammal, reptile, or bird.

claw.e: From Middle English clawen, from a combination of Old English clawan/clāwan (a remodelling of *clīeġan, from Proto-West Germanic *klauwjan, from Proto-Germanic *klawjaną) and Old English clawian (from Proto-West Germanic *klawēn).
claw.g: To scratch or to tear at.

clay.e: From Middle English cley, clay, from Old English clǣġ (“clay”), from Proto-West Germanic *klaij, from Proto-Germanic *klajjaz (“clay”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *gleyH- (“to glue, paste, stick together”). Related also to clag, clog.
clay.g: A mineral substance made up of small crystals of silica and alumina, that is ductile when moist; the material of pre-fired ceramics.

clean.e: From Middle English clene, from Old English clāne, clǣne (“clean; pure; clear”), from Proto-West Germanic *klainī (“dainty, fine, small; clean”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *glēy- (“gleaming”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to gleam”).
clean.g: Free of dirt, filth, or impurities (extraneous matter); not dirty, filthy, or soiled.

cleanness.e: From Old English clǣnnes, corresponding to clean + -ness.

cleanse.e: From Middle English clensen, from Old English clǣnsian, from Proto-West Germanic *klainisōn, from Proto-West Germanic *klainī (“clean”).
cleanse.g: To free from dirt; to clean, to purify.

clear.e: From Middle English clere, from Anglo-Norman cler, from Old French cler (Modern French clair), from Latin clarus.

clearer.g: Someone who or something which clears.

clearly.e: From Middle English clerli, clerely, clerelych, cleerliche, clerliche. By surface analysis, clear + (adverbial) -ly.

clearness.e: From Middle English clernesse; equivalent to clear + -ness.

cleave.e: From Middle English cleven, from the Old English strong verb clēofan (“to split, to separate”), from Proto-West Germanic *kleuban, from Proto-Germanic *kleubaną, from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ- (“to cut, to slice”).
cleave.g: To split or sever something with, or as if with, a sharp instrument.

cleave.e: From Middle English cleven, a conflation of two verbs: Old English clifian (from Proto-West Germanic *klibēn, from Proto-Germanic *klibāną) and Old English clīfan (from Proto-West Germanic *klīban, from Proto-Germanic *klībaną), both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gleybʰ- (“to stick”).
cleave.g: Followed by to or unto: to adhere, cling, or stick fast to something.

cleft.e: From Middle English clifte, from Old English ġeclyft, from Proto-West Germanic *klufti, from Proto-Germanic *kluftiz, equivalent to cleave + -t (“-th”). The modern form with /ɛ/ is by association with Etymology 2 (the past form of cleave).
cleft.g: An opening, fissure, or V-shaped indentation made by or as if by splitting.

clemency.e: From Middle English clemency, clemencie, from Latin clēmentia. Gradually eclipsed Middle English clemence, from Old French clemence, from the same Latin origin.
clemency.g: The gentle or kind exercise of power; leniency, mercy; compassion in judging or punishing.

clerk.e: From Middle English clerc, from Old English clerc, from Late Latin clēricus (“priest, clergyman, cleric”, also generally “learned man, clerk”), from Ancient Greek κληρικός (klērikós, “of the clergy”, adj. in church jargon), from κλῆρος (klêros, “lot, inheritance”, originally “shard used in casting lots”).
clerk.g: One who occupationally provides assistance by working with records, accounts, letters, etc.; an office worker.

clever.e: From East Anglian dialectal English cliver (“expert at seizing”), from Middle English cliver (“tenacious”). perhaps from Old English *clifer, clibbor (“clinging”); or perhaps from Dutch, Low German, or East/Saterland Frisian (compare kluftich (“clever, prudent”), probably derived from Proto-West Germanic *kleuban (“to cleave, split”)).
clever.g: Nimble with hands or body; dexterous; skillful; adept.

client.e: From Middle English client, from Anglo-Norman clyent, Old French client, from Latin cliēns, akin to clinare (“to lean”).
client.g: A customer, a buyer or receiver of goods or services.

cliff.e: From Middle English clyf, from Old English clif, from Proto-West Germanic *klib, from Proto-Germanic *klibą.
cliff.g: A vertical (or nearly vertical) rock face.

clift.e: Variant form of cliff, influenced by cleft.

climb.e: From Middle English climben, clymben, from Old English climban (“to climb”), from Proto-West Germanic *klimban, from Proto-Germanic *klimbaną (“to climb, go up by clinging”), believed to be a nasalised variant of Proto-Germanic *klibaną, *klibāną (“to stick, cleave”), from Proto-Indo-European *gley- (“to stick”).
climb.g: To traverse a slope or contour, either upwards (ascending) or downwards (descending).

climbing.e: From Middle English clymbyng, clymbynge; equivalent to climb + -ing.
climbing.g: The sport of climbing, ascending a wall or a rock or another object using available holds, generally with the safety of a rope and belayer.

cling.e: From Middle English clingen, from Old English clingan (“to adhere”), from Proto-West Germanic *klingan, from Proto-Germanic *klinganą.
cling.g: Fruit (especially peach) whose flesh adheres strongly to the pit.
To produce a high-pitched ringing sound, like a small bell.

clip.e: From Middle English clippen, cleppen, clüppen, from Old English clyppan (“to hug, embrace, cherish, clasp”), from Proto-Germanic *klumpijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *glemb-, *glembʰ- (“lump, clump, clod, clamp”).
From Middle English clippen, from Old Norse klippa (“to clip, cut the hair, shear sheep”).
clip.g: To cut, especially with scissors or shears as opposed to a knife etc.

cloak.e: From Middle English cloke, from Old Northern French cloque (“travelling cloak”), from Medieval Latin clocca (“travelers' cape, literally “a bell”, so called from the garment’s bell-like shape”), of Celtic origin, from Proto-Celtic *klokkos, ultimately imitative.
cloak.g: A long outer garment worn over the shoulders covering the back; a cape, often with a hood.

clod.e: From Middle English clod, a late by-form of clot, from Old English clot, from Proto-West Germanic *klott (“mass, ball, clump”). Alternatively, Middle English clod may derive from Old English *clod (found in Old English clodhamer (“a kind of thrush”) and Clodhangra (a placename)), from Proto-West Germanic *kloddō (“lump, clod”).
clod.g: A lump of something, especially earth or clay.

close.e: From Middle English closen (“to close, enclose”), partly continuing (in altered form) earlier Middle English clusen (“to close”) from Old English clȳsan (“to close, shut”); compare beclose, foreclose, etc.), and partly derived from Middle English clos (“close, shut up, confined, secret”, adjective), from Old French clos (“close, confined”, adjective).
close.g: To remove or block an opening, gap or passage through.

close.e: Borrowed from French clos, from Latin clausum, participle of claudō.
close.g: Having little difference or distance in place, position, or abstractly; see also close to.

closer.e: From Middle English closere, equivalent to close (verb) + -er.

closet.e: From Middle English closet, from Old French closet, from clos (“private space”) + -et (diminutive suffix), from Latin clausum. Equivalent to close + -et, but generally applied in French solely to small open-air enclosures.
closet.g: A small room within a house used to store clothing, food, or other household supplies.

cloth.e: From Middle English cloth, clath, from Old English clāþ (“cloth, clothes, covering, sail”), from Proto-West Germanic *klaiþ, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą (“garment”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *gleyt- (“to cling to, cleave, stick”) (compare Albanian ngjit (“to stick, attach, glue”)), a form of *gleh₁y- (“to smear; to stick”).
cloth.g: A fabric, usually made of woven, knitted, or felted fibres or filaments, such as used in dressing, decorating, cleaning or other practical u

clothe.e: From Middle English clothen, from Old English *clāþian (“to clothe”), from Proto-Germanic *klaiþōną (“to clothe”), from Proto-Indo-European *gley- (“to adhere to, stick”).
clothe.g: To adorn or cover with clothing; to dress; to supply clothes or clothing.

clothing.e: From Middle English clothing, clathing, from Old English *clāþung, from Proto-West Germanic *klaiþungu (“clothing”), equivalent to clothe + -ing.
clothing.g: Any of a wide variety of articles, usually made of fabrics, animal hair, animal skin, or some combination thereof, used to cover the human b

cloud.e: From Middle English cloud, from Old English clūd (“mass of stone, rock, boulder, hill”), from Proto-West Germanic *klūt, from Proto-Germanic *klūtaz, *klutaz (“lump, mass, conglomeration”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to ball up, clench”). Largely replaced Middle English welkne, from Old English wolcn (whence English welkin).
cloud.g: A visible mass of water droplets suspended in the air.

cloudless.e: From Middle English cloudeles, equivalent to cloud + -less.

cloudy.e: From Middle English cloudy (“cloudy, overcast, gloomy, dark", also "hilly, rocky”), from Old English clūdiġ (“stony, rocky”), equivalent to cloud + -y.
cloudy.g: Covered with or characterised by clouds.

clout.e: From Middle English clout (“piece of cloth”), from Old English clūt (“piece of cloth, patch; metal plate”), from Proto-West Germanic *klūt, from Proto-Germanic *klūtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gelewdos, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to ball up, amass”). The influence sense originated in the dialect of Chicago, but has become widespread.

club.e: From Middle English clubbe, from Old Norse klubba, klumba (“cudgel”), from Proto-Germanic *klumpô (“clip, clasp; clump, lump; log, block”).
club.g: A heavy object, often a kind of stick, intended for use as a bludgeoning weapon or a plaything.

cluster.e: The English word is probably a doublet of clot.
cluster.g: To collect (animals, people, objects, data points, etc) into clusters (noun sense 1).

clutch.e: From Middle English clucchen, clicchen, cluchen, clechen, cleken, from Old English clyċċan (“to clutch, clench”), from Proto-West Germanic *klukkjan, from Proto-Germanic *klukjaną, from Proto-Germanic *klu- (“to ball up, conglomerate, amass”), from Proto-Indo-European *glew- (“to ball up; lump, mass”).
clutch.g: To seize, as though with claws.

clutch.e: Variant form of cletch, from Middle English cleken (“to hatch”), perhaps from Old Norse klekja (“to hatch”).
clutch.g: A brood of chickens or a sitting of bird, monotreme or reptile eggs; a sitting.
